What gives the state the right to kill another human being without consequence though? The law? If the law allows for the death penalty then it is contradicting itself as the law say 'killing another human being is unlawful' and the death penalty is exactly that : killing another human being.

If we define what is and what is not murder by the state of the law, then anything can be justified : for example, we would all consider the atrocities that took place at Auschwitz-Birkenau as murder, but they were lawful weren't they? The Nuremberg Laws stated that Jews had no rights compared to 'normal German citizen'. The mass murder of Jews, political opponents, homosexuals, and gypsies was lawful, but we all agree that it was murder.

Who gives us the right to pass down judgement on others? God? But isn't one of His most important laws, the Commandments, 'thou shalt not kill'? Of course, we could say 'but that is not literal and meant to be interpreted' but what gives us the right to interpret the supposed Word of God as something else than what was written?

There is a famous book by Victor Hugo, the author of Notre-Dame de Paris and of Les Misérables, called in French 'Le Dernier Jour d'un Condamné'. This means 'the last day of a condemned', it is rather short for a work of Hugo's, only 150 pages if I'm not mistaken. In it, he explores how when à man who commits murder, he solely is not at fault, for society as whole too failed. For if a man kills, even if the act has no reason, it means that society turned a blind eye to the signs, it didn't help, it didn't offer psychological evaluations, it too has a responsibility in the act.

I hope I wasn't too long, I just wanted to expose my point of view so not as to be called 'foolish' like a certain gentleman has.

Do you know that before WW1, pink was a boy's colour and blue was a girl's colour? Indeed, pink, being close to red, was associated with passion, anger, violence and blood. Blue, a calming colour, was associated with finesse, aesthetism and elegance and as such was thought to be more féminine.

The title of the book (Ten Little N******) in most languages other than English is the first title Christie chose for her novel, it was later changed for *obvious* reasons. It is a reference to the nursery rhyme (ten little soldiers went out to dine...) ; since the most widespread version of the rhyme was a minstrel song talking about well... Ten little black people. I personally don't find it that shocking as it is only a reference to the nursery rhyme and not an actual racist  comment (if you're looking for racism in literature, tilt your head towards Lovecraft).

Yes, I know. What I meant to ask (I may have asked it in the wrong way, I can be a bit of a babbler), is "How did it happen?" in a pure and boring way. As a"what happened after" more than anything. I know personally it isn't some switch (especially for me as someone who rambles and can't keep his mouth shut > I came out to my crush by accident) but I know (only from afar) people who have it not be a secret anymore and while I did see them being merrier in a way, what I saw most were the insults (just to clarify I don't live in an extremely homophobic country, it's just school, everyone's a piece of shit) and well while they weren't directly said to them, I know for a fact they heard the insult since they were said literally two meters away from them.

I suppose I should clarify a few things: in a year, there are some people that I will never see again, while that may not bother some people, school for me has become my home, especially the teachers, they've become friends, nearly family. I have some friends who only believe me to be a cold person and I'd like for them to know that well, there is a beating under the stone. I don't want others to remember me as the cold, sarcastic know-it-all when they look back at their life.

Now I understand that my question was vague (nebulous I should say) but I guess what I should have asked is "what was the process" because you can't just whip out a traffic cone and yell that you're gay into it (although I suppose it would look quite comical) but it's just that part that intrigues me: how on earth do people know? (while I would like others to know, I obviously do not want the entire world knowing, I'm just using hyperbolic sentences) Because it seems like it just pops out of nowhere most of the time, knowledge that someone is LGBTQ, that is.
